Explore the eight plans

Open all eight plans. Each one protects against a different physical risk.

0/8

Select a region to see its details.

Fire Safety Plan

Purpose: Protect people from harm caused by fire and smoke.

Main functions: Prevention and routine inspections · Detection and suppression systems · Code Red response (RACE/PASS) · Evacuation routes and drills

Building Safety Plan

Purpose: Keep the physical environment free of hazards.

Main functions: Environmental and safety rounds · Hazard identification and correction · Construction/renovation risk assessment · Safety signage and wayfinding

Hazmat & Waste Plan

Purpose: Safely manage chemicals and medical waste end to end.

Main functions: Inventory, SDS and GHS/NFPA labelling · Safe storage, handling and transport · Code Orange spill response · Waste segregation and disposal

Utility Plan

Purpose: Keep essential utility systems running safely.

Main functions: Critical system inventory · Preventive maintenance · Backup power and water continuity · Code Brown response

Biomedical Plan

Purpose: Make sure medical equipment is safe and working.

Main functions: Equipment inventory and inspection · Planned preventive maintenance (PPM) · Incident and recall management · User training

Security Plan

Purpose: Protect people, property and information.

Main functions: Access control and ID badges · Visitor and contractor management · CCTV monitoring · Response to Codes White, Silver, Black and Pink

Internal Disaster Plan

Purpose: Prepare for emergencies that start inside the facility.

Main functions: Emergency code activation · Emergency Response Team (ERT) roles · Continuity of critical services · Regular internal drills

External Disaster Plan

Purpose: Prepare for mass-casualty or community events.

Main functions: Surge capacity planning · Coordination with Civil Defence, MOH and Red Crescent · Code Yellow triage and communication · Community drills

Incident types

Open each incident type.

Near miss — most valuable to report

Nothing happened, but it easily could have. Reporting it is free learning.

First aid case

Minor injury treated with on-site first aid; no further medical care.

Medical treatment case

Needs treatment beyond first aid, such as stitches or prescribed medication.

Lost time injury

The employee cannot return to normal duties for a period.

Fatality

Death from a workplace incident; triggers mandatory investigation and regulatory reporting.

The AREC cycle

AREC is a habit before every task. Hazard awareness is never a one-time task.

1Anticipate — think ahead before the task
2Recognise — spot hazards as they appear
3Evaluate — how likely, how severe
4Control — use the hierarchy, top first
Noor: AREC as a habit before every task, not a form. Read each label as a prompt for what to check or who should act next. The useful step is linking the visual with a real decision. Good habits here are quiet: check, confirm, continue. Pause and connect this to your role. Use the principle in context. Keep the next action clear. Think of the first detail you would check.

Hierarchy of controls

Put the controls in order, from most to least effective.

  1. Elimination — physically remove the hazard
  2. Substitution — replace it with something safer
  3. Engineering controls — isolate people from the hazard
  4. Administrative controls — change how people work
  5. PPE — protect the individual worker
Noor: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose. Use the rule you practised.

The trailing cable

Noor · Safety liaison

A power cable trails across the walkway beside the patient waiting area. Patients and visitors are walking past.

Score: 0

You spot the cable. What do you do first?

  • Best choice. You recognised the hazard and protected people first. Now evaluate it and choose a control.

  • Not safe. A trip hazard beside patients is everyone's responsibility. Recognising it and doing nothing leaves the risk in place.

  • Reporting matters, but not before people are protected. Someone could trip while you are away.

Which control is strongest?

  • Strongest. Removing the hazard from the walkway sits at the top of the hierarchy — nobody can trip on it.

  • Better than a sign, but the cable is still in the walkway. Removing it from the path is stronger.

  • A sign is an administrative control. It relies on people noticing it, so it is weaker than removing the hazard.

  • Warning people is the weakest option here. It depends on you being there every time.

Your supervisor says: “Leave it, we're busy.” What do you do?

  • Correct. Under ISO 45001 you can stop work you believe could cause serious harm, without fear of retaliation. Your Safety Liaison is the bridge to EHS.

  • The hazard is still there. Your rights exist so that safety concerns are never silenced by fear of consequences.

  • The concern is valid, but raise it through the right route: stop the unsafe work and contact your Safety Liaison or Safety Officer.

Who to contact and your rights

Who to contact, and your rights under ISO 45001.

Department Safety Liaison

Your first contact for hazards, risk assessments and PPE questions. Don't know yours? Ask your supervisor on day 1.

Right to stop unsafe work

Stop any task you believe could cause serious harm, without fear of retaliation.

Right to be consulted

If you are afraid to stop work yourself, raise the concern with your Safety Officer or supervisor.

Right to training

Be trained on the hazards and safe procedures of your role before you do it.

The common response pattern

Put the common response pattern in order. It applies to every code.

  1. Recognise — notice the emergency as it develops
  2. Activate — call switchboard/security; announce the correct code
  3. Respond — follow your role-specific response
  4. Stand down — wait for the official all-clear

The fire triangle

Remove any one side and the fire stops. Smoke, not flame, is the leading cause of death in facility fires.

1Heat — the ignition source
2Fuel — anything that burns
3Oxygen — keeps it burning
Noor: Remove one side of the triangle and the fire stops. Smoke kills first, which is why RACE rescues and contains before extinguishing. RACE: put the steps in order

You discover a fire. Put the response in the right order.

  1. Rescue anyone in immediate danger
  2. Alarm — pull station + call: code, location, your ID and name
  3. Contain — remove O₂ and alcohol rub, close doors
  4. Extinguish a small fire, or Evacuate
Noor: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose.

PASS: put the steps in order

Using an extinguisher: put the PASS steps in order.

  1. Pull the safety pin
  2. Aim low, at the base of the fire
  3. Squeeze the handle
  4. Sweep side to side until it is out

Find the fire safety equipment

Open every item. Know where these are before you need them.

0/8

Select a region to see its details.

Smoke detector

Senses smoke early and triggers the alarm. Never cover or tamper with it.

Heat detector

Triggers the alarm when the temperature rises fast — used where smoke detectors would false-alarm.

Sprinkler

Releases water automatically over a fire. Keep the space below it clear; never hang anything from it.

Call point

Manual alarm. Pull it during the Alarm step of RACE.

Fire extinguisher

For a small, contained fire only. Check the class label, then use PASS.

Fire blanket

Smothers a small fire, such as a pan or clothing fire, by cutting off oxygen.

Evacuation chair

Moves a person who cannot walk down the stairs during a vertical evacuation. Never use the elevator.

Assembly-point sign

Shows the route to the outdoor assembly point used in a full evacuation. Find yours this week.

Types of evacuation

Three types of evacuation.

Move patients and staff through fire/smoke doors to the next safe compartment on the same floor. The first response for most fires.

Move to a lower floor or ground level when horizontal is not enough. Use stairwells, never elevators.

Evacuate the whole building to the outdoor assembly point. Only for the most severe, facility-wide emergencies.

Noor: Horizontal first. Vertical by stairs. Full evacuation only for the worst events. Use the tabs as a short reference, not a checklist to race through. Choose the evacuation

Smoke is coming from Room 3. Fire doors are at the end of the corridor. Patients on the same floor are not in danger yet. What is your first move?

Correct. Horizontal evacuation is the first response for most fires: the fire doors hold back smoke.

Never use elevators in a fire. They can fail or open onto the fire floor; vertical moves use the stairwells.

Too early. Full evacuation is for the most severe, facility-wide emergencies; moving patients beyond the fire doors is enough now.

Night shift: put RACE into action

Noor · Safety liaison

Night shift. Smoke is rising from a waste bin in a patient room. The patient is in bed beside it.

Score: 0

What do you do first?

  • Rescue first. The patient is safe from the smoke before anything else happens.

  • The patient stayed in the smoke while you were away. Smoke kills first, so rescue comes before extinguishing.

  • The alarm matters, but the patient was left beside the fire. Rescue anyone in immediate danger first.

You pull the call point and phone switchboard. What do you say?

  • Correct. Code type, exact location, your ID and name — the team can come straight to you.

  • Without the code and location the team loses time finding you. Always state code, location, ID and name.

  • Code Orange is a hazardous spill. A fire is Code Red; the wrong code sends the wrong team.

The patient is safe and the alarm is raised. How do you contain the fire?

  • Correct. Removing oxidisers and flammables and closing the door slows the smoke and fire.

  • Opening a window feeds the fire with oxygen. Close doors and windows to contain it.

  • An open door lets smoke spread down the corridor. You gave the location on the call; close the door.

The fire spreads past the bin. Smoke reaches the corridor. What now?

  • Correct. The fire is no longer small and contained, so you evacuate. Horizontal is the first move.

  • An extinguisher is only for a small, contained fire. Once it grows, evacuate.

  • Never use elevators in a fire. Move horizontally first; use the stairwells if you must go down.

Read a diamond

Store, handle, transport

Everything follows the Safety Data Sheet (SDS).

Storage per SDS

Away from incompatible substances, secured, away from heat sources.

Designated carts and routes

Never carry incompatible chemicals together; secure containers before moving them.

PPE per SDS

Wear the PPE the SDS specifies before opening, mixing or dispensing.

Flammable cabinet

Double-walled steel with a self-latching door. Flammable liquids never go on an open shelf.

SDS at point of use

An SDS pocket or binder at or near the cabinet — every SDS reachable in seconds.

Spill or Code Orange?

Noor · Safety liaison

Three spills, three decisions. Use the rule you'd follow on shift. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

Score: 0

A 200 mL bottle of alcohol hand rub falls and leaks in the corridor.

  • Correct. It is below the Code Orange threshold and not highly toxic. Keep people away until it is cleaned. Draft rule: 500 mL or more, or any highly toxic, reactive or explosive substance. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

  • Not needed here. Code Orange is for spills at or above the threshold (draft: 500 mL), or highly toxic, reactive or explosive substances. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

A full 1-litre bottle of surface disinfectant splits and spreads across the treatment-room floor. (Over the draft threshold. ⚠ Draft — pending D1)

  • Correct. The spill is over the threshold, so it needs the Code Orange response. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

  • A spill this size needs Code Orange and the right spill kit and PPE, not paper towels. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

A few millilitres of a highly toxic reagent spill on a lab bench.

  • Correct. Volume does not matter for a highly toxic substance: any amount is Code Orange. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

  • Small volume, but highly toxic. Any highly toxic, reactive or explosive substance is Code Orange. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

Code Orange is called. Which order do you follow?

  • Correct. Protect people first, protect yourself, then contain with the chemical or biological kit, and report to your supervisor and Safety Services.

  • Containing before isolating and protecting yourself puts you and others at risk. Isolate and warn first.

  • PPE must go on before you touch the spill, and people nearby need warning first. Report at the end.

Security rules

Security rules for people and premises.

  • ID always — wear your facility ID at all times.
  • Contractor permits — a valid, approved work permit before any work starts.
  • Visitor badges — visitors sign in at reception. Report anyone in a restricted area without one.
  • CCTV covers public areas, entrances and parking.
  • Lost and found — hand found items to Security.
  • Designated parking only.
  • No smoking anywhere, including entrances and parking.

The visitor without a badge

A man without a badge is in the staff-only medication room. He says he is a contractor. What is the best action?

Correct. Contractors need an approved permit and ID. Calling Security without leaving him alone protects the medicines.

Risky. Anyone can say they are a contractor; without a permit and badge he should not be in a restricted area.

That leaves him alone with the medicines. Call Security from where you are and stay with him.

An unbadged person in a restricted area must be reported. Security needs to know, even if he leaves.

The overdue infusion pump

Dr. Omar · Family physician

A busy ward. You are about to set up an infusion pump. Its inspection label is two months overdue.

Score: 0

Inspection due: March. Today: May (fictional training dates). Do you use the pump?

  • Correct. A pump past its inspection date is not known to be safe today.

  • Working is not the same as safe. Never use equipment past its due date.

What do you do with the pump?

  • Correct. The tag stops a colleague from using it by mistake.

  • Untagged, the next person may use it. Tag it out of service.

  • Never attempt your own repair or bypass a fault. That is Biomedical Engineering's job.

Who do you notify?

  • Correct. Biomedical Engineering runs the PPM programme and will inspect it.

  • Inspection and PPM are coordinated by Biomedical Engineering. Report to them.

  • IT handles network outages, not medical equipment. Notify Biomedical Engineering.

A colleague says: “Just take the pump from Room 5, nobody's using it.” What do you do?

  • Correct. Each location is assessed for the equipment placed there. Never relocate equipment without Biomedical Engineering, even temporarily.

  • Even a temporary move bypasses the location assessment. Coordinate with Biomedical Engineering first.

True or false? Store oxygen cylinders upright and secured, with full and empty clearly separated.

Ionising vs non-ionising

Radiation is energy travelling as waves or particles.

X-ray, CT. Enough energy to remove electrons from atoms: needs dosimeters, shielding and dose tracking.

MRI, ultrasound, laser light. Lower energy, but still needs its own precautions.

The magnet is always on. No metal objects, oxygen cylinders or unscreened staff. Screening every time.

Wear a lead apron during exposure. Stand behind the shield or leave the room.

Laser hazards and measures

Hazards

  • Eyes — permanent damage, often with no pain at first
  • Skin — burns from direct or reflected beams
  • High voltage inside the equipment

Measures

  • Eye protection
  • Beam management
  • Control reflections
  • Training
Noor: Laser eye injuries often don't hurt at first — that's why protection is not optional. Keep the main point connected to a familiar task or conversation. One shift, three plans

Noor · Safety liaison

One afternoon shift. Three things go wrong. Your decisions decide how it ends. No timer — take your time. You have 3 lives and one hint per situation.

Score: 0♥ 0⏱ 0

1 · 14:10. In a busy clinic, a cleaner knocks over a large 1-litre bottle of surface disinfectant. It spreads towards an oxygen cylinder. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

  • Right. Over the draft threshold, so Code Orange; and oxygen must be kept away from hazards. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

  • A spill this size needs Code Orange, the right kit and PPE per the SDS. You lost a life. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

  • The hazard and the oxygen cylinder are still next to people. Isolate and warn first. You lost a life.

2 · 15:30. The alarm sounds. Smoke is coming from the store room, and a patient is waiting in the chair beside the door.

  • Right. Smoke means Code Red, and RACE starts with rescue.

  • Smoke means fire: Code Red. The wrong code sends the wrong team. You lost a life.

  • The patient is still beside the smoke. Rescue comes before extinguishing. You lost a life.

3 · 17:00. All clear. Dr. Omar needs suction for a patient and you notice the suction unit's inspection label has expired.

  • Right. Dr. Omar: “That is the habit we want from every new colleague.”

  • Working is not the same as safe. Never use equipment past its due date. You lost a life.

  • Never relocate equipment without Biomedical Engineering, and the expired unit is still untagged. You lost a life.

Debrief: one shift, three plans

  • The spill — Hazmat & Waste plan (Code Orange), with Fire Safety (oxygen kept away).
  • The smoke — Fire Safety plan (Code Red, RACE) and Internal Disaster (code activation).
  • The suction unit — Biomedical plan (inspection label, out-of-service tag, Biomedical Engineering).
